headline: Outgoing at 1 A.M.: Bass Hold the Deep Hole, Weakfish Wake Up at the Bridge
subhead: With the neap tide softening the current, the Night Owl worked the back half of the ebb and found the bite he'd been waiting on.
body_markdown:
I made the call Wednesday night to skip the dusk incoming and wait for the outgoing to really get moving past midnight. That's the thing about this inlet — everybody shows up at sunset, dumps bunker chunks off the jetty rocks for an hour, and clears out by ten thinking the bite's over. It isn't over. It's just getting started for guys willing to sit in the dark until the tide really starts pulling.

The first-quarter neap on the 21st has been softening the current all week, and that's changed the timing on the deep hole east of the Coast Guard station. Normally on a big spring push you get one tight window right at max ebb where the bass stack up on the sand eels getting swept through. With the current running softer this week, that window's stretched out — I had fish from about 1 a.m. through almost 3, working a 3-ounce bucktail with a white 6-inch Fin-S trailer, bouncing it slow along the bottom where the deep hole drops off the sandbar. Nothing huge — mostly 26 to 32 inches, a few slot fish mixed with shorts — but steady enough that I never went more than fifteen minutes without a hit. Live eels drifted on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current seam did about as well, and if you want a bigger fish, that's the bait I'd reach for. The bass are here on the nocturnal program right now — the back bay's been running warm, mid-to-upper 70s off the flats by Tiana, and that pushes the bigger stripers into feeding at night and staying deep and quiet through the heat of the day. We flagged this pattern building last week, and it's held — the warm water squeezed the bite into low light, and that's exactly what's playing out at the inlet.

Ponquogue Bridge is where the real story is this week, though. Weakfish had gone quiet through the hot stretch in early July, but the calm, settled evenings we've had — light southwest wind, clean water, no chop pushing through the inlet — brought them back. I had three keeper weakfish Thursday night on the outgoing, fishing bucktails tipped with squid strips right in the bridge shadow where the current breaks around the pilings. Small chartreuse bucktails, half-ounce, bounced right on bottom in about 18 to 22 feet, worked slow so the current does the swimming for you. A few guys working the same stretch with Berkley Gulp swimming mullets in pink shad picked up weakfish too, along with some decent porgies mixed in on the drift closer to the channel edge. This is the pattern we said would rebuild on calm warm nights, and it did — but I want to be honest, it's not a slam dunk yet. Some nights it's three fish in three hours, other nights you work the whole tide and get one bite. The window's real, but it's still thin. Fish the last two hours of the outgoing under the bridge lights and don't be surprised if the bite comes in one short burst rather than a steady pick.

Fluke fishing in the bay has been the most dependable thing going, day or night, and that's held true out here same as everywhere else on the South Shore right now. Drifting the flats off Tiana Beach and out toward the canal mouth in 8 to 14 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter-ounce bucktails have been putting keeper fluke in the boat, a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds. The channel edges along the west side of the bay toward Hampton Bays are holding fish too — bigger baits, squid strips over bucktails, worked slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still moving bait across the structure. This is a daytime program mostly, which makes for a nice complement if you're out there grinding bass and weakfish through the dark hours — sleep in, fluke fish the afternoon flood, then go back out for the night bite.

Bluefish have been sporadic inside the inlet, nothing like the blitzes happening up around the bunker schools further west, but there's enough bait pushing through on the tide changes that you'll run into cutoffs and slashing fish working topwater plugs off the rocks at first light. If bunker schools push further east along the barrier beach the way they've been trending, expect that to change fast — worth keeping an eye on the surf reports from the west.

As for the canal — the connection to the Peconic has been quiet for stripers this week, mostly small blues and a scattering of porgies working the current there, nothing worth a special trip yet. That could change once water starts moving more with the tide building back toward full moon.

Looking ahead, the softening currents from this neap should keep stretching out the productive windows at the inlet — more time on the bite, if less raw power in the tide. If the calm evenings hold, I'd keep working the bridge on the outgoing for weakfish, and I'd keep the deep hole in play for bass after midnight. If a front comes through and stirs the water, that bridge bite could shut off fast, so take advantage of the calm while it's here.
